title: Why Almost Every Airline Has Sued This One Website
protagonist: the host as a cheapskate traveller (with Skiplagged as the underdog); airlines are the antagonist
want: fly Denver to New York cheaply; airlines want the website dead
central_question: Airlines keep suing this website and losing. Why can't they kill it, and how did they create it?

beats.text: A traveller flies two legit Lufthansa tickets.
Years later Lufthansa sues him for about $2,400.
The culprit is hidden-city ticketing and a site airlines try and fail to sue to death, because it is not illegal.
Host demo: the nonstop he wants costs $324.
A cheaper one-stop to another city starts with that exact flight; just skip the second leg.
Scale: millions of users, tens of millions a year kept from airlines, so they hate it.
Blame flips: the airlines built the incentive, not the website.
Deregulation leads to hub-and-spoke networks.
Nonstops are cheaper to fly yet priced higher; hub monopoly vs non-hub competition explains the cheap fare.
Airlines knowingly discount connecting seats to fill planes; skiplagging breaks that balance.
It is legal, like card counting; airlines can only use terms of service, and almost never do.
So they sue the website instead (two big suits).
One wins only on logo copyright; the other is dismissed: still not illegal.
They will keep suing and failing unless they price against their own model; literary-parody sting.

loops.q: Why would an airline sue a man for skipping a flight? (case dismissed)
Why can't airlines sue the website out of existence?
How did airlines create hidden-city ticketing?
What is hidden-city ticketing?
What's the first leg of my cheap Boston flight?
Why is the nonstop pricier when it's cheaper to run?
How are airlines supposed to crack down on this?

turns: 2:38 blame reversal: the website didn't create the problem, airlines did
3:27 counter-intuitive: the product people want most costs the airline least
6:42 the opening lawsuit gets dismissed
7:19 the big win is only about a logo
ending: Answer: airlines can't win without breaking their own pricing. Last line is a Great Gatsby parody about losing $180 at a time, then 'there are worse things'. Callback to the cold-open lawsuit.

title: Why Rolex Won't Sell You Their Most Expensive Watches
protagonist: Amy, the host's 'outside correspondent', on a doomed shopping mission
want: buy a platinum Daytona off the shelf
central_question: Why is walking into Rolex and buying its top watch impossible?

beats.text: Amy is sent to a boutique to buy the priciest Daytona.
Her mission is doomed: not money, not her stained sneakers, but the ownership structure.
Origin: founder builds the brand.
Wanting it to outlive him, he hands 100% to a nonprofit foundation.
Myth-bust: Rolex is both for-profit and not, at once.
No shareholders, no quarterly pressure, so no reason to meet demand.
Surely someone buys it from Rolex? No online store, display-only shelves.
Amy asks; no advisor slots; best case an 'expression of interest' waitlist of years.
The waitlist isn't a queue; you must prove loyalty by buying lesser watches.
A huge secondary market; a watch flips for far over retail the same day.
Twist: the fastest way to buy Rolex's top watch is to not buy from Rolex and pay more.
Why is Rolex fine leaving that money? Profits go to the foundation anyway.
Luxury is about access too (other brands do it).
Rolex is unique: secret, low-tax, profit-distant, so no incentive to change. Wry sting.

loops.q: Why is Amy's mission doomed?
Why is that employee counting all the watches?
What's a perpetual trust? (joke answer, then real one)
Surely someone buys it from Rolex?
How long is the waitlist?
What if you're an investor, not a collector?
Why does Rolex tolerate the resale market?

turns: 0:06 'mission doomed' fake reasons before the real one
1:37 both common beliefs about Rolex are wrong
4:52 the retail price reveal derails the narrator
5:28 the way to buy from Rolex is not to buy from Rolex
ending: Central answer delivered as a moral ('no incentive to do it any other way'), closing on a wry 'may we all be so lucky'. Amy's quest is never formally closed; it is resolved by the twist.

title: How Iran Smuggles 777 Airplanes
protagonist: Iran / Mahan Air, running a heist
want: get modern wide-body jets despite a total ban
central_question: Nobody may sell Iran a Boeing, yet it got five. How do you smuggle five tracked jumbo jets?

beats.text: Iran's airline launches routes with shiny new 777s.
This is illegal; US sanctions office panics.
Nobody can sell Iran a Boeing, yet it got five, after years. How?
Why they must smuggle: US export rules reach any plane with 10% US parts, so every wide-body.
No new planes or parts; aging, dangerous fleet; smuggling is the only option.
Target: five retired jets in a desert boneyard.
Step 1: a near-invisible US company buys and registers them.
Step 2: parked in China, sold to a shell in Madagascar; oversight weakens.
Step 3: moved to Cambodia; now nobody is watching.
Final step is hardest: still US-made, and Iran may only host them 72 hours.
Crime: an expired ferry permit to Kenya gets its month scribbled over.
Convoy flies; over loosely watched airspace the transponders switch off; jets vanish.
They land in Iran; nobody can be sanctioned because the shell isn't real. Happily ever after.

loops.q: Why is this illegal?
How do you smuggle five wide-body jets?
Why does Iran need to smuggle planes at all?
Is this buyer even a real company?
How do they get past the last border?
How do you fly without a valid route?

turns: 0:12 good-news launch flips to 'this is illegal'
3:50 laundering done, but the hardest step remains
4:51 transponders off, planes vanish
5:15 nobody to punish because the company isn't real
ending: Heist completes; ironic fairy-tale close ('lived happily ever after').

title: Why It's Illegal to Call a Drug "Stroebenazoline"
protagonist: the host as boss of a fake pharma company
want: name his left-nostril decongestant and sell it
central_question: Who decides drug names, and why are so many names banned? Let's try to name ours.

beats.text: Pharmacy roll-call of real names; some invented names are banned.
Naming is a rule-heavy process run by several bodies.
Mission: name our own absurd one-nostril drug.
Stakes: look-alike names cause deaths and injuries every day.
Generic name = stem (what it does) + prefix; attempt 1 uses the channel name.
Rejected: too long, banned first letter, promotes a channel.
More attempts, each with two violations; back-and-forth with regulators and a similarity tool.
A generic name finally passes after a public objection window.
Now the brand name, for profit, under a different regulator.
Attempt fails: copies the generic and uses a stem.
Attempt fails: sounds like an existing antidepressant.
Attempt fails: trademarked, and a real case where one name meant two drugs abroad.
Attempt fails: promises results and contains numbers.
A plain name passes the basics, then the similarity checklist is a coin-flip; ends unresolved.

loops.q: How do we name our drug? (generic)
Why does a drug have three names?
How will the name start?
What will the regulators say?
Can we get a brand name approved?
Will this one work?
Might we finally be in business?

turns: 1:13 a silly naming game becomes life-and-death
2:02 the meaningful-looking syllables mean nothing
5:43 same brand name, different drug in another country, real hospitalisation
7:21 the 'safe' name may still fail
ending: Generic solved, brand name left in limbo; host jokes he may have to pay the consultant after all. New question left open, used as sponsor bridge.

title: This Is The Shortest Train in the United States
protagonist: the Dinky (an object) and the town it serves
want: survive; Princeton wants a link to the main line
central_question: Why does Princeton get its own 3-mile train, and why keep it?

beats.text: Longest US passenger route: days across the country.
Contrast: the shortest is an 8-minute hop nicknamed the Dinky.
Anywhere else this would be a shuttle bus or a few Ubers. Why a train?
Correction: an even shorter line existed until 1957.
The Dinky exists because of the big Northeast Corridor.
Corridor built in pieces along a canal; Princeton had a nearby stop, no Dinky needed.
The twisty canal route was too slow once the Civil War raised demand.
Line straightened; Princeton left 3 miles off the map (huge in the 1860s).
1865: the Dinky opens (comically bad early trains).
Cars arrive, yet the Dinky expands (football crowds).
The university it serves keeps shortening it, building over the terminal three times.
Replacement debate: the terminal is on campus, not downtown.
Counter-case: it only needs to meet trains, and replacing it costs ~7x maintaining it.
It survives as a Civil War-era compromise; sting about reopening the shorter rival.

loops.q: How did Princeton end up with its own branch?
Why have they kept it?
Was it always the shortest?
Why move the main line?
How did it survive the car?
Do we still need it?

turns: 1:13 'shortest' title claim gets a caveat
3:03 a faraway war reroutes the line and strands the town
4:17 the car era makes it grow, not shrink
4:29 its own beneficiary keeps cutting it shorter
ending: Both halves answered; 'for now the Dinky survives'. Callback to the shorter rival line as the last joke, then sponsor bridge.

title: The Weird, Scary Airspace Over Washington DC
protagonist: the host as a stray pilot, then 'you' the airline pilot
want: land at DC's airport without being intercepted or losing a licence
central_question: Hundreds of flights land here daily without getting shot at. What does it take, and what if you mess up?

beats.text: Host tours DC by air; a light flashes.
He's in restricted airspace; an F-16 pulls up.
Yet 800+ airliners a day land here unharmed. How?
Layer 1 rules: clearance, ID code, transponder.
Layer 2: an inner zone that needs a waiver.
Stray in and an escalation ladder starts: cameras, lasers, radio, helicopter sign, fighters.
So strict that emergencies must divert elsewhere.
Even that isn't the strictest: prohibited zones over the White House and VP home (licence, jail).
So planes must snake along rivers, direction set by wind.
North flow: easy arrivals, hard-turn departures.
South flow: a straight approach crosses the forbidden zone, so pilots follow river bends and turn at 200 ft.
And that runway is the nation's busiest; simultaneous land-and-takeoff; trainee controllers quit.
Get it all right: coolest job. Get it wrong: worst day, and you see an F-16 up close.

loops.q: What's that flashing light?
How do airliners land here safely?
What happens if you screw up?
Just how serious is it?
Why is the approach so tricky?
What else are pilots dealing with?

turns: 0:24 danger zone is also a daily commute
2:27 the scary zone isn't even the strictest
4:41 the normal straight approach would end your career
5:43 'and that's not even all'
ending: Resolved as a two-sided verdict; final image calls back to the cold-open F-16.

title: WW2 - OverSimplified (Part 1)
protagonist: Hitler (with Mussolini and Japan as fellow wanters) vs the Allies
want: the dictators want to undo humiliation and grab territory; the Allies want to avoid another WW1
central_question: Implicit, carried by dramatic irony: how do these grudges become a world war, and can anyone stop Hitler? (no explicit question in the first 30 s)

beats.text: Mussolini: draft-dodging socialist, arrested again and again.
He flips to pro-war, gets expelled, invents fascism.
Italy feels cheated after WW1, so he grabs power.
Germany humiliated by Versailles; Hitler rises on that anger; same enemies make them friends; Japan joins (its own grudge with the West).
Hitler breaks the treaty step by step; Allies do nothing, twice.
Allies appease: Austria, then Sudetenland, signed promise.
He takes the rest of Czechoslovakia anyway.
Allies draw a line at Poland; Hitler secures his back with Stalin; invasion; war.
Phony War: France is still fighting WW1, Britain drops leaflets.
Norway fiasco; Chamberlain out, Churchill in.
Everyone expects a WW1 replay; Blitzkrieg through the 'impenetrable' forest; France falls; Dunkirk.
Britain refuses to quit; Hitler tries isolation mind-games; air war nearly breaks the RAF.
A tiny raid on Berlin enrages Hitler; he switches to bombing London.
RAF regroups and wins; invasion postponed; 'shot himself in the foot, just the foot for now'.

loops.q: What will the newly pro-war Mussolini do?
Who is this new friend (Japan) and what does it want?
Will appeasement hold?
Will the Allies really fight for Poland?
Will anyone actually fight?
What's Hitler's trick up his sleeve?
Will Britain give up?
Is the invasion coming? (but then...)
'Just the foot for now': how does Hitler fully self-destruct? (Part 2)

turns: 1:54 anti-war socialist becomes pro-war nationalist
7:10 the signed promise is broken
8:13 Hitler-Stalin pact stuns the West
10:47 expected WW1 replay becomes Blitzkrieg
12:51 the villain's anger at a small raid saves Britain
ending: Britain survives, invasion postponed. Last line foreshadows Hitler's later blunders: a deliberate open loop into Part 2.

title: The Cold War - OverSimplified (Part 1)
protagonist: the US and Stalin's USSR (later Khrushchev, Kennedy)
want: USSR wants a buffer of loyal states and to spread communism; the US wants to contain it
central_question: Wartime friends are now suspicious: will they end up in a nuclear war? (planted 2:21 'something's up with Stalin')

beats.text: 1917: Germany sends Lenin home to wreck Russia (Lennon mix-up gag).
Revolution, chaos; dying Lenin warns against Stalin, who controls appointments; stalin takes over through purges.
WW2 allies win, but Stalin seems ominous; the bomb reveal falls flat: his spies already knew.
Promised free elections become puppet states; Iron Curtain.
Tug-of-war over Greece, Turkey, Iran; NATO; Truman Doctrine = Cold War declared.
Stalin bets misery breeds communism; THEREFORE the US floods Europe with aid; Stalin builds rivals.
Berlin blockade, answered by the airlift; Stalin backs down.
The Soviets get the bomb; war now 'inevitable'; China goes communist.
Korea: invasion, comeback, MacArthur swears China won't come; it does; stalemate.
Stalin dies of his own terror; successor promises freedom, then crushes uprisings and bans jazz.
Spies everywhere, Red Scare, U-2 shot down.
USSR seems ahead in space and missiles; H-bombs; Warsaw Pact.
Easterners flee via Berlin; Kennedy's slip ('East Berlin is yours') lets Khrushchev build the wall.
Tank standoff at the checkpoint; both inch back from apocalypse; 'biggest crisis?' It wasn't.

loops.q: Who is the soldier meant to fetch?
Who did Lenin put in charge of jobs?
What's up with Stalin / will the allies fall out into war?
Will the bomb scare Stalin?
How did he already know?
Will the elections be free and fair?
What will the West do about the blockade?
What happened to China?
Will China get involved?
So how did de-Stalinization work out?
How will Khrushchev stop the defections?
Will the tank standoff go nuclear?
What is the bigger crisis coming? (Part 2)

turns: 2:46 the big reveal is old news to Stalin
4:14 'free and fair' elections are rigged
9:15 the general's promise is broken instantly
9:52 the tyrant's terror kills him
10:19 liberalisation turns into crackdowns
14:06 replay exposes Kennedy's slip that enables the wall
ending: Standoff defused comically ('one more inch'), then a sting line that opens the next crisis. Cliffhanger, not resolution.

title: WW2 - OverSimplified (Part 2)
protagonist: Hitler (and Japan) at the peak, vs the Allies
want: Hitler wants the USSR's land and oil; Japan wants resources; the Allies want to survive then win
central_question: Britain isn't alone, the Axis looks unstoppable: what turns it around? (Part 1's 'just the foot for now' carries over)

beats.text: Correction: Britain wasn't alone; alliances shift.
Mussolini tries three conquests, each worse than the last.
Hitler shores up the south; the US stays out but sends weapons.
U-boats could starve Britain; THEREFORE better tech and code-breaking.
Hitler launches the largest invasion ever; staggering gains to Moscow.
Winter; he refuses to dig in; cold-trained troops push him back.
Japan needs resources, so it must first destroy rival navies: Pearl Harbor.
It missed the fuel and subs; Hitler needlessly declares war on the US; victories 'built on speed, not power'.
Cocky Hitler splits his forces for oil; one army must take Stalingrad.
Soviets had moved factories east; they encircle the army; Hitler forbids retreat; surrender.
Reversals everywhere: Africa, Midway, Burma, Italy topples Mussolini.
D-Day: deception and a weather window; France liberated.
Desperate Hitler repeats his old forest trick; 'Nuts'; it fails.
Berlin falls; Okinawa; the bomb; Japan surrenders; two superpowers set up a 'very cold' war.

loops.q: Was Britain really alone?
Will Italy finally shine?
Can U-boats starve Britain?
Will Hitler take Moscow?
How can Japan beat the US and UK navies?
Was Pearl Harbor really a big win?
When will power catch up with Japan?
Where will the invasion land?
Will Hitler's old trick work twice?
Invade Japan or force surrender?
What will the two superpowers' 'cold' war be? (next series)

turns: 4:05 the unstoppable army meets winter
5:31 the 'huge victory' missed the key targets
7:09 hidden Soviet factories flip Stalingrad
9:35 deception: the enemy guards the wrong beach
11:36 the villain repeats his greatest hit and it fails
ending: Axis destroyed; aftermath image (emperor shown as human). Last line plants the next conflict: a 'very, very cold' war.

title: The American Revolution - OverSimplified (Part 1)
protagonist: the colonists (later Washington) vs King George and Britain
want: colonists want to keep self-rule and not be taxed without a say; Britain wants its war debt paid and control
central_question: Britain is broke and wants the colonies to pay: how does a tax fight become a revolution, and can amateurs beat the world's best army?

beats.text: Columbus finds gold; the race for the New World begins.
France builds forts on land Britain claims; Washington's skirmish sparks a world war.
Britain wins but is broke.
Asks the colonies to chip in; they say no; so taxes.
No say in Parliament: boycotts, Britain repeals.
Vain king repeats it; repeals again except tea; sends troops.
Heckling escalates (snowballs to rocks); soldiers fire; massacre; tea dumped in the harbor.
Britain takes direct rule; colonies meet, ask Britain to stop, get no, arm militias.
Raid on rebel arms; first shot; best army flees farmers; Boston besieged; a fort seized.
Washington made commander; costly British 'win' at Bunker Hill.
What are they fighting for? Peace letter; king answers with insults.
Callback: the seized guns are hauled 300 miles; Britain must leave Boston.
A pamphlet makes independence mainstream; Declaration; no turning back.
Huge British fleet; flank trap; defeat after defeat; fog escape; the army barely survives.

loops.q: Why is Columbus yelling at the monarchs?
Will France stop building forts?
Will the colonies pay Britain back?
What will the broke king try now?
Boston tension about to come to a head: how?
What to do about the British?
What happens to the fort's captured guns?
What happens to the snubbed Benedict Arnold?
Why are they even fighting?
When will the British attack?
Is the war already lost?
Can the beaten army fight another day? (Part 2)

turns: 2:25 victory leaves the winner broke
4:16 the king repeats a policy that just failed
8:02 the world's best army flees farmers
12:15 guns appear on the heights overnight: checkmate
14:08 the battle was a decoy; the real force flanks
ending: Army crushed yet alive; final line 'rarely beaten so badly yet survived'. Unresolved cliffhanger into Part 2.

title: WW1 - Oversimplified (Part 1)
protagonist: the great powers, mainly Germany and its plan
want: each nation wants 'stuff' (land back, more land, navy prestige); Germany wants a fast win in the west then the east
central_question: Everyone wants a war: how does it start, and will Germany's lightning plan work?

beats.text: Civilised 1914, 'let's have a war'; each nation's want in a line.
Archduke rides an open car on a published route through hostile land.
The bombers miss; fake-out 'and the war never happens'.
He goes back out, wrong turn, stalls by an assassin; shot.
Ultimatum, war on Serbia; alliances drag everyone in.
Britain says 'maybe' and stays out, good for Germany's plan.
French forts; so Germany goes through neutral Belgium.
Belgium fights back and Britain joins after all.
Atrocities and propaganda sway America.
Old-style tactics and bright uniforms meet modern guns.
Russia is ready early; Austria-Hungary flops, even against Serbia.
Germans in sight of Paris, then a gap opens; they retreat.
Race to the sea, stalemate, trench lines coast to Switzerland.
How trench warfare works and its horror; sincere close.

loops.q: How will the publicised drive go?
Fake resolution: war averted? (except no)
Will Britain back France?
'Just one problem': how to get past French forts?
Will Belgium just let them through?
Spot the French soldier: who else spotted him?
Can Austria-Hungary handle Russia?
Will Germany get its quick win after all?
How long will the trenches last? (Part 2)

turns: 0:53 fake-out 'the war never happens'
1:07 coincidence chain kills the Archduke
2:42 the 'sit down and shut up' neutral fights
4:44 near-victory collapses into retreat
ending: No resolution; switches to a sincere description of trench horror. Open into Part 2.

title: The French Revolution - OverSimplified (Part 1)
protagonist: weak King Louis XVI vs the starving Third Estate
want: Louis wants to be left alone and keep the party going; the people want bread and a fair say
central_question: France is broke and the poor carry everything: 'what are they gonna do, revolt?' (sarcastic plant at 2:02)

beats.text: Royal wedding: awkward prince, France broke, 'fat ill-bred boy' chorus.
France's glamour rests on a starving 80%; 'revolt? nah'.
Lost war with Britain, debt; the nobles party harder; peasants pay.
A soaked drunk asks 'why?': the Enlightenment; weak Louis inherits the mess.
Funds the American Revolution for revenge; never repaid; deeper debt; queen's spending and royal ridicule; monarchy respect at a low.
The fix: tax the poor (salt-tax sketch).
Bad harvests; bread soars; riots.
Louis dodges: summons a long-dormant assembly.
Voting: 98% of people get one vote of three.
Third Estate forms its own assembly; locked out, swears an oath in a tennis court.
Radicals want no king; the king moves troops; fear everywhere.
Now or never: arms seized, the Bastille stormed, governor's head on a pike; assembly embraces the violence; a bathtub agitator stokes it.
A great rights declaration, but people are still starving.
Women march on the palace; 'let them eat cake'; the king submits and moves to Paris.

loops.q: Can this weird boy handle being king of a broke France?
What are the poor gonna do, revolt?
When will America pay France back?
What could push them over the edge?
What decisive action will the king take?
Any ideas to fix the money? / how will voting work?
Locked out: what will they do?
Where to get gunpowder?
Has the governor won?
Denounce the violence or embrace it?
What will starving people do next?
What happens to the king now? (Part 2)

turns: 2:02 sarcastic 'revolt? they're only 80%' sets dramatic irony
3:41 the ally never repays
8:41 98% of the people get a third of the votes
9:55 the lock-out simply moves them to another building
12:48 the 'winning' governor's head is on a pike
13:14 reformers choose violence
ending: The king gives in and returns to Paris: the separation that caused the problem is removed. Open into Part 2.
